newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin in hospital all week, but stable - doctor.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin in hospital all week, but stable - doctor.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin is recovering from pneumonia but the Kremlin's top doctor has described his illness as treacherous and urged him to stay in hospital at least to the end of the week.

The 65-year-old Kremlin leader, reported last Friday to be depressed at falling ill so soon after surviving heart surgery, also faced trouble from political opponents who are trying to kick him out of the Kremlin on health grounds.
"I should say that this is a fairly serious illness, which of course brings with it a whole range of possible complications," chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov told a news conference on Wednesday.
"I think that he should stay in the Central Clinical Hospital...until the end of this week. Beyond that it will depend on the course of his illness," he said.

He said Yeltsin had wanted to stay in hospital for three days after he was admitted late last Wednesday and though his condition had "stabilised considerably" he had been persuaded that he needed more time there.

Yeltsin's opponents, citing the president's absences from work particularly since his quintuple heart bypass on November 5, are seeking to carve a path through Russia's legal labyrinth to remove him from office on health grounds.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said his party, the biggest in parliament, would decide on Thursday whether to back moves to oust Yeltsin -- though they are unlikely to succeed.

"The president last year worked four months -- only during the election campaign -- and on the whole he didn't focus on government affairs but on promises," Zyuganov, who lost to Yeltsin in last July's presidential election, told reporters.
"For any citizen of the country it raises the question: 'Why isn't there any leadership in the country?"'.
But Mironov, referring to Russian labour law which counts a period of sickness from the date when an invalid last worked, said Yeltsin had officially only been off work for a week.

Yeltsin at first had been confined to bed but was now working on documents, he said. "Sometimes he gets up at 3.30, 4 o'clock and works on documents and then three hours later he might sleep for another hour and a half."
"Of course we try to limit his workload because the illness he now has is quite treacherous," he said.
One big complication such a patient could develop was waterlogging in the lungs, or pulmonary oedema, Mironov said.
"It was one of the reasons he was taken to hospital, because it is a very dangerous situation, especially with double pneumonia," he said, referring to inflammation in both lungs.
The doctor also spoke of potential deterioration in the heart muscle due to the pneumonia, which had also been avoided.
"But of course the illness leaves its mark on all organs and systems and lung disease, of course, is close and linked to cardiac problems," he added.

Russian debt prices slumped to their lowest for a month and traders said the market would remain volatile until more was known about Yeltsin's illness, which comes on top of heart problems which kept him from the Kremlin for six months.

The threat from Yeltsin's opponents looked set to continue. Communist Viktor Ilyukhin, head of parliament's security committee, said he would press for a vote on Friday to force Yeltsin out, though experts said this would have no legal force.
The constitution is vague on removing an ailing head of state, saying only that the president "ceases his functions" if his health is too weak, without specifying who would decide.
